People love to attack this kind of writing. They call it cowardly. They say it exists so that nobody has to take responsibility, and I understand why it sounds that way, but I want to defend it for one specific document. A public safety notice is about the product. It is not about me and it is not about the person who approved the batch in November. The moment you put a name in that notice, the reader stops doing the only thing the notice exists for, which is checking whether they own one of the affected units, and starts looking for somebody to be angry with. That is a worse outcome for everybody, including the person you just named. Now, the internal report is a completely different animal, and I want to be clear about this. That one has names in it. It has dates. It has who signed off on what, line by line, and it is the document that gets read if anybody is ever held accountable. Two documents. Two jobs. The mistake people make is judging one of them by the standards of the other.

A researcher at a business school ran a study that is very simple and slightly uncomfortable. Two groups of participants read an incident report about a product failure. The reports were word for word identical except in one sentence. In the first version, a named manager approved the batch. In the second version, the batch was approved. That is the entire difference. One name, present or absent. The group who read the version with no name estimated a substantially lower financial cost for the incident, and they were markedly less likely to say that anybody should lose their job over it. Now here is the part I find genuinely interesting. The finding does not tell you anything about the writer's intentions. It does not prove that anybody was hiding anything. The effect is exactly the same whether the form was chosen deliberately to protect somebody, or whether the writer simply wrote the way reports have always been written in that company. The sentence does the work either way, and the reader has no way of knowing which one it was. That is the reason to know about it, whichever end of the document you are standing at.
